mc_sub: Read every saved run: pick one to inspect it, or select several to see how a change (features, SMOTE, label mode) moved each model.
mc_none: No runs yet. Train models on the Pipeline Runner and the results will appear here.
mc_cv_note: Bars show mean accuracy; the whisker is the standard deviation across folds. If whiskers overlap, the models are not clearly different.
mc_cm_help: Rows are the true class, columns the predicted class. Each cell shows the count and the share of that true class. A strong diagonal means few mistakes.
mc_cm_weak: The hardest class for this model is {c}: only {v:.1f}% of its samples are recognised.
mc_cmp_help: Select two or more runs to compare. Compare runs of the same dataset and label mode; change only one thing between runs to see its effect.
mc_not_comparable: These runs use different datasets or label modes, so the numbers are not directly comparable.
mc_no_metric: The selected runs have no value for this metric (for example, no cross-validation).
cr_sub: Train on one dataset and test on another to see whether a detector still works on data it has never seen.
cr_purpose: Why this page: a model that scores 99% on its own dataset can fail on another one, because each dataset is collected differently. Here a model is trained on dataset A using only the columns whose names also exist in dataset B, then tested on dataset B. The drop from the in-dataset score to the cross-dataset score shows how well the model generalises. Labels are simplified to Benign vs Malware so datasets with different malware classes can be compared.
cr_need_two: Add at least two datasets to use this page.
cr_shared_n: {n} shared column names (dataset A has {a}, dataset B has {b}).
cr_err_shared: The two datasets share no column names, so a model trained on one cannot be applied to the other.
cr_shared_hint: Rename columns in your CSV so equivalent features have the same name, then upload it again.
cr_few: Very few shared columns; the result may be weak or unstable.
cr_shared_note: Columns with the same name are assumed to measure the same thing. Exclude any column you suspect has a different meaning in the two datasets.
cr_cfg: Run #{id} · train {a} → test {b} · {n} shared columns · {rows} test rows
cr_read_good: {m} keeps its performance on {b}: macro F1 goes from {i:.1f}% to {x:.1f}% (drop {d:.1f} points). The learned patterns seem to transfer well.
cr_read_mid: {m} loses some performance on {b}: macro F1 goes from {i:.1f}% to {x:.1f}% (drop {d:.1f} points). It partly transfers, but results on {a} overstate what to expect on new data.
cr_read_poor: {m} does not transfer well: macro F1 falls from {i:.1f}% to {x:.1f}% (drop {d:.1f} points) on {b}. High scores on {a} mostly reflect that dataset's own characteristics.
cr_read_missed: Only {r:.1f}% of the malware in the test dataset is detected, so many malicious samples would be missed.
cr_read_falsealarm: Only {s:.1f}% of benign samples are recognised, so many harmless samples would be flagged as malware.
cr_read_prior: The share of malware differs a lot between the datasets ({a:.0f}% vs {b:.0f}%), which also affects the scores.
cr_read_caveat: This tests one direction on the columns they have in common. Swap train and test to check the other direction.
cr_cm_help: Predictions on the test dataset only. Rows are the true class, columns the predicted class.
cr_err_class: Each dataset needs at least 10 Benign and 10 Malware samples.
